reasoning: All six failure-driven edits are kept. They fix persistent failures through shared mechanisms: strike clue-supplied words, class-versus-variety names, possessive owner, quoted-word compounds, short fragments, and acronym or superlative handling. None collides with the protected block or weakens Rule 3's verbatim-archive override. The four success-driven edits cover patterns the failure edits do not: dictionary-headword definitions, shared-title or work-title slots, proverb completion, and archive category headers as wordplay hints. I kept them at lower priority because they add separate coverage rather than duplicating failure fixes. The two edits that insert after the same 'One of these <role/title>' anchor (possessive owner and shared title) address different clue shapes, so both stay. All anchors are exact strings from the current skill and sit outside the SLOW_UPDATE markers.

edits.target: - DELETE-CLUE-WORDS TEST: before answering, strike from your candidate every specific word or phrase the clue already states, and keep only the remaining head.
edits.content: - DELETE-CLUE-WORDS TEST (mandatory; name the struck words in your one reasoning line): before answering, strike from your candidate every specific word or phrase the clue already states, including ordinals and numbers ('the third leader to bear this title' -> 'Dalai Lama', not 'third Dalai Lama') and any first name, title or nickname the clue supplies ('the only president named Chester' -> 'Arthur', not 'Chester A. Arthur'; 'his name was Zeb, but others called him this' -> the alternate name only, not alternate + 'Zeb'). Keep only the remaining head. For 'called / known as / nicknamed this' clues, the answer is ONLY the alternate name or title, never the alternate plus the original name.

edits.target: Modifiers copied from passages (hot air, synthetic, funeral, speech) are usually wrong unless part of the standard proper name.
edits.content: Modifiers copied from passages (hot air, synthetic, funeral, speech) are usually wrong unless part of the standard proper name. This includes species and variety prefixes (Sea, Common, Atlantic, Great): when the clue describes a whole class ('this freshwater, jawless fish'), answer the class name ('Lamprey'), not the one variety a passage happens to discuss ('Sea lamprey').

edits.target: - 'One of these <role/title>' ('the 14th one of these spiritual leaders') asks for the title or category noun itself (Dalai Lama), not the individual named in the clue.
edits.content: - POSSESSIVE OWNER: in 'X & Y are in this organization's Hall of Fame, founded in 1967', 'this country's capital', 'this company's founder', the slot is the OWNER (organization, country, company), not the possessed thing the clue already names. A candidate repeating 'Hall of Fame' is wrong. Pick the owner whose own facts match the clue's other details and give its short common name or acronym.

edits.target: - A word in quotation marks inside the clue (a 'drag', a nickname) is usually a pun or hint tied to the answer. Look for passages where that word appears next to a candidate and answer with that candidate.
edits.content: - A word in quotation marks inside the clue (a 'drag', a nickname) is usually a pun or hint tied to the answer. Look for passages where that word appears next to a candidate and answer with that candidate. A quoted word plus 'of them' ('a "city" of them') signals a compound: search the passages for 'X-town', 'X city', 'X-ville' and similar, and answer X. A multi-part clue ('Slang for a pub, it's also a shack; ...') defines ONE word several ways. The answer must fit EVERY part, so never take an unrelated headword from a slang or glossary list just because it appears there.

edits.target: If the list is of real people, answer with the team, state or other entity they share.
edits.content: - Short fragments with no verb (use only when no verbatim archive answer exists, Rule 3): a lone quoted catchphrase or exclamation ('Yabba Dabba Do!') asks for the character, show or franchise it is famous from, not an episode or product whose title merely contains the words. A bare single place name ('Hamburg') asks for the country (or U.S. state) that contains it, never the place itself. A bare '"Title" (year)' film or play fragment asks for the one person the passages credit with making it, usually the director, not a cast member.

edits.target: - Ask: what category is the answer (country, person, vitamin, object, band), and what member of that category fits all the clue details?
edits.content:
- ACRONYM in the clue ('If your TV has PIP, it has this feature'): when the clue contains an abbreviation and asks for 'this feature / term / thing', the answer is usually the spelled-out expansion, taken from a passage that prints 'Picture-in-Picture (PIP)', not a stray phrase from a forum question or side remark.
- SUPERLATIVES: name the dimension being measured. 'Smallest in size' (physical dimensions) is not 'lowest value', 'lightest' or 'oldest'. Check the candidate against your own knowledge of the real measurements rather than choosing the best-known or lowest-denomination item.

edits.target: A dictionary synonym that fits only one half ('trial') is wrong. When passages are noisy, use your own knowledge of sports terms and idioms.
edits.content: - BARE-DEFINITION clues ('It can mean to emit vapor or to show irritation', "the part of a racetrack from the last turn to the finish line") ask for the dictionary HEADWORD that the definition glosses. Look for dictionary-style passages ('Define X', 'X - definition', 'X | Merriam-Webster') that repeat the clue's wording; the word in their titles is the answer. Give it bare, in the form that fits the definition (verb for 'to ...', noun for 'the part of ...'). A synonym that appears only inside the definitions is wrong.

edits.target: - 'One of these <role/title>' ('the 14th one of these spiritual leaders') asks for the title or category noun itself (Dalai Lama), not the individual named in the clue.
edits.content: - 'Title / office / rank held by A, B & C' (people from different countries or eras) asks for the ONE shared title noun, not a listed person or a country. Use the title the passages pair with every name. 'In this book / play / film / opera' plus a character or plot detail asks for the WORK's standard title, not the character, the author or the scene. Choose the title the passages repeat beside the named character and plot detail.

edits.target: answer with the common English name (Conch).
edits.content: - Proverb, saying or quotation clues, where a pronoun or 'this' stands for a blanked word of the saying, ask for the missing word. Recall the full saying and answer with only the missing word. If the passages merely echo the clue, rely on your own knowledge of the saying.

edits.target: - Archive lines may also be formatted 'CATEGORY | clue text | answer'. Take the answer that follows the clue, even if the whole context is one short passage.
edits.content: - If an archive passage shows the clue under a category header but no answer, the header is a hint. A wordplay category ('DOUBLE "D"s', 'rhymes with...', 'starts with a body part') constrains the answer's spelling or sound, so test your candidate against it. A page that only repeats the clue (quiz-spam titles, solver listings) is not an archive hit. Fall back to passages that paraphrase the clue's facts, or to your own knowledge.
